happen if the line is crossed. Thus R should come
before S6.

questions.solution:
Commercial black powder looks black because the little
lumps of the stuff are coated with graphite. In the
manufacturing process, the powder's mixed with water
or some other liquid binder, pressed into cakes and
dried, then crushed and screened into powders of

burn. The graphite serves no chemical purpose, but it
lubricates the particles, and also makes the bulk powder
electrically conductive enough that it is unlikely to
initiate proceedings unexpectedly because of a staticelectricity
spark.

The following 8 (Eight) items consist of two statements, Statement I and Statement II. You are to examine these two statements carefully and select the answers to these items using the code given below :

Statement II : The acceleration due to gravity of the earth decreases with height.
options: Both the statements are individually true and Statement II is the correct explanation of Statement I
Both the statements are individually true but Statement II is not the correct explanation of Statement I
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is true but Statement II is true
questions.solution:
Mass is an invariant quantity. Acceleration due to gravity (g) decreases with altitude as one rises above the Earth's surface because greater altitude means greater distance from the Earth's centre.
Weight, $\mathrm{w}=$ mass $(\mathrm{m}) \times$ acc. due to gravity $(\mathrm{g})\mathrm{g}_{\text {height }}=\mathrm{g} /\left(1+\frac{\mathrm{h}}{\mathrm{R}}\right)^2$
Hence body weighs less on hill top than on earth's
surface.

questions.q: If radius of the earth were to shrink by $1 \%$, its mass remaining the same, g would decrease by nearly
questions.solution:
If the radius of the earth were to shrink by one percent, mass remaining the same, the value of $g$ will increase by $2 \%$.
$\mathrm{g}=\frac{\mathrm{GM}}{\mathrm{R}^2}$
If mass remains constant, then $\mathrm{g} \propto \frac{1}{\mathrm{R}^2}\begin{aligned}
& \% ~\text { increase in } g=2(\% ~\text { decrease in } \mathrm{R}) \\
& =2 \times 1 \%=2 \%
\end{aligned}$
Therefore value of g will increase by $2 \%$.

questions.q:
The sun is observed to be reddish when it is near the horizon,
i.e., in the morning and the evening. This is because
options: red light is least scattered by atmosphere
red light is most scattered by atmosphere
it is the colour of the Sun in the morning and evening
questions.solution:
Tiny molecules in our atmosphere cause light to scatter. That's why our sky looks blue: it's because the atmosphere scatters the bluish component of white sunlight. And it's why the sun looks reddish when it's near the horizon. Sunlight encounters more air molecules when the sun is low in the sky than when the sun is overhead. Even more blue light is scattered away, leaving mostly the reddish scattering
$\propto \frac{1}{\lambda^4}$ component of white sunlight to travel the straighter path to your eyes. So the setting and rising sun looks red.

questions.subject: General Ability
questions.q:
When you walk on a woolen carpet and bring your finger
near the metallic handle of a door an electric shock is
produced. This is because
options: charge is transferred from your body to the handle
a chemical reaction occurs when you touch the handle
the temperature of the human body is higher than that of the handle
the human body and the handle arrive at thermal equilibrium by the process
questions.solution:
All materials are made up of negatively- and positivelycharged particles. These usually exist in equal amounts, balancing each other out. But when two materials come into contact, one may 'steal' negatively-charged
electrons from the other. One material ends up with more negative charges than positive ones, meaning that it becomes negatively-charged overall, whilst the other becomes positively-charged. If the charges cannot move away as they are produced, they accumulate in the material as static charge, or electricity. Once you have built up a big enough static charge, an electric shock is almost inevitable. The moment you touch a conducting material such as metal, the excess electrons jump between your hand and the conductor, giving you a shock.

questions.q: To a perpendicular to the plane of ecliptic, Earth's axis of rotation makes an angle of $23 \frac{1}{2}$ degrees. Had this angle been zero degree, which one among the following would result ?
options: There would have been no season
The length of day and night would have been the same throughout the year
The length of the day and night would have been the same all over the earth
questions.solution:
In astronomy, axial tilt (also called obliquity) is the
angle between an object's rotational axis and the
perpendicular to its Orbital plane, both oriented by the
right hand rule. At an obliquity of 0°, these lines point
in the same direction i.e. the rotational axis is
perpendicular to the orbital plane. Axial tilt differs from
inclination. Over the course of an orbit, the angle of
the axial tilt does not change, and the orientation of
the axis remains the same relative to the background
stars. This causes one pole to be directed toward the
Sun on one side of the orbit, and the other pole on the
other side, the cause of the seasons on the Earth.

What is the solution of the differential equation $\frac{d x}{d y}+\frac{x}{y}-y^2=0$ ?
where $c$ is an arbitrary constant.
questions.solution:
$\begin{aligned}
& \frac{d x}{d y}+\frac{x}{y}-y^2=0 \\
& \frac{d x}{d y}+\frac{x}{y}=y^2
\end{aligned}$
This is a linear differential equation of the form
$\frac{\mathrm{dx}}{\mathrm{dy}}+\mathrm{P}_1 \mathrm{x}=\mathrm{Q}_1$
Here, $\mathrm{P}=\frac{1}{\mathrm{y}}$ and $\mathrm{Q}=\mathrm{y}^2\therefore \quad \text { I.F. }=\mathrm{e}^{\int P d y}=\mathrm{e}^{\int \frac{1}{y} d y}=\mathrm{e}^{\log y}=y$
So, required solution is
$\begin{aligned}
& x \cdot y=\int y^2 \cdot y d y+c \\
& x y=\int y^3 d y+c \\
& x y=\frac{y^4}{4}+c \\
& 4 x y=y^4+c
\end{aligned}\therefore \quad$ Option (C) is correct.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q:
Consider the following statements:
1. The general solution of $\frac{d y}{d x}=f(x)+x$ is of the form $y=g(x)+c$, where $c$ is an arbitrary constant.
2. The degree of $\left(\frac{d y}{d x}\right)^2=f(x)$ is 2 .
Which of the above statements is/are correct?
questions.solution:
Statement 1:
The general solution of $\frac{d y}{d x}=f(x)+x$ 
Now integrating on both side
$\int \frac{d y}{d x}=\int[f(x)+x] d x\therefore \quad y=f(x)+C\therefore \quad$ Statement 1 is correct.
Statement 2:
$\frac{d y}{d x}=f(x)+c$
Squaring both sides,
$\begin{aligned}
& \left(\frac{d y}{d x}\right)^2=(f(x)+c)^2 \\
& \left(\frac{d y}{d x}\right)^2=\left[f(x)^2+2 \mathrm{cf}(x)+c^2\right]
\end{aligned}$
Hence, the differential equation is of order -1 and degree -2 .
$\therefore \quad$ both Statements 1 and 2 are correct.
$\therefore \quad$ Option (C) is correct.

What is the solution of the differential equation
$\sin \left(\frac{d y}{d x}\right)-a=0 ?$
where $c$ is an arbitrary constant.
questions.solution:
$\begin{aligned}
&  \sin \left(\frac{d y}{d x}\right)-a=0 \\
& \sin \left(\frac{d y}{d x}\right)=a \\
& \Rightarrow \quad \frac{\mathrm{dy}}{\mathrm{dx}}=\sin ^{-1} \mathrm{a} \\
& d y=\sin ^{-1} a d x \\
& \text { Now integrating both sides, } \\
& \int d y=\int \sin ^{-1} a d x \\
& y=x \sin ^{-1} a+c \\
& \therefore \quad \text { Option (A) is correct. }
\end{aligned}$

Given that $\frac{d}{d x}\left(\frac{1+x^2+x^4}{1+x+x^2}\right)=A x+B$
What is the value of A?
questions.solution:
Given $\frac{d}{d x}\left(\frac{1+x^2+x^4}{1+\mathrm{x}+\mathrm{x}^2}\right)=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{dx}}\left[\frac{1+\mathrm{x}+\mathrm{x}^2+\mathrm{x}^4-\mathrm{x}}{1+\mathrm{x}+\mathrm{x}^2}\right]\begin{aligned}
& =\frac{d}{d x}\left[1+\frac{x^4-x}{x^2+x+1}\right] \\
& =\frac{d}{d x}\left[1+\frac{x\left(x^3-1\right)}{x^2+x+1}\right] \\
& =\frac{d}{d x}[1+x(x-1)] \\
& =\frac{d}{d x}\left[1+x^2-x\right]=2 x-1...(i)
\end{aligned}$
Now comparing equation (i) with $\mathrm{AX}+\mathrm{B}$, we get $\mathrm{A}=2$ and $\mathrm{B}=-1$.

questions.q: The angles of elevation of the top of a tower standing on a horizontal plane from two points on a line passing through the foot of the tower at distances 49 m and 36 m are $43^{\circ}$ and $47^{\circ}$ respectively. What is the height of the tower?
questions.solution:
$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{AB}=\mathrm{h} \text { (height of the tower) } \\ & \mathrm{BD}=36 \mathrm{~m} \\ & \mathrm{BC}=49 \mathrm{~m} \\ & \angle \mathrm{D}=47^{\circ} \\ & \angle \mathrm{C}=43^{\circ}\end{aligned}$
Now, in $\triangle A B D$, $\tan 47^{\circ}=\frac{\mathrm{h}}{36 \mathrm{~m}}...(i)$ and in $\triangle \mathrm{ABC}$, $\begin{aligned} & \tan 43^{\circ}=\frac{\mathrm{h}}{49 \mathrm{~m}} \\ & \tan \left(90^{\circ}-47^{\circ}\right)=\frac{\mathrm{h}}{49} \end{aligned}\therefore \quad \cot 47^{\circ}=\frac{\mathrm{h}}{49}...(ii)$ Multiplying equations (i) and (ii) $\begin{aligned} & \tan 47^{\circ} \cdot \cot 47^{\circ}=\frac{\mathrm{h}}{36} \times \frac{\mathrm{h}}{49}=1=\frac{\mathrm{h}^2}{36 \times 49} \\ & \mathrm{~h}=6 \times 7=42 \mathrm{~m} \end{aligned}\therefore \quad$ Option (B) is correct

questions.solution:

Hyperbola passes through $(3 \sqrt{5}, 1)\begin{aligned}
\therefore \quad & \frac{(3 \sqrt{5})^2}{\mathrm{a}^2}-\frac{1}{\mathrm{~b}^2}=1 \\
& \frac{45}{\mathrm{a}^2}-\frac{1}{\mathrm{~b}^2}=1...(i)
\end{aligned}\begin{aligned}
& \text { Now length of latus rectum }=\frac{2 b^2}{a} \\
\Rightarrow & \frac{4}{3}=\frac{2 b^2}{\mathrm{a}} \\
\Rightarrow & \frac{2}{3}=\frac{\mathrm{b}^2}{\mathrm{a}} \Rightarrow \mathrm{a}=\frac{3 \mathrm{~b}^2}{2}...(ii)
\end{aligned}$
Putting the value of ‘a’ from equation (ii) in equation (i),
$\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow \quad \frac{45 \times 4}{9 b^4}-\frac{1}{b^2}=1 \\ & \Rightarrow \quad \frac{20}{b^4}-\frac{1}{b^2}=1\end{aligned}\begin{aligned}
& 20-b^2=b^4 \\
& b^4+b^2-20=0 \\
& b^4+5 b^2-4 b^2-20=0 \\
& b^2\left(b^2+5\right)-4\left(b^2+5\right)=0 \\
& \left(b^2-4\right)\left(b^2+5\right)=0 \\
& b^2=4, b^2=-5 \\
& \therefore \quad b^2=4 \Rightarrow b=2
\end{aligned}$
Now length of conjugate axis
$=2 b=2(2)=4\therefore \quad$ Option (C) is correct.

questions.q:
The integral $\int \frac{d x}{a \cos x+b \sin x}$ is of the form $\frac{1}{r} \operatorname{In}\left[\tan \left(\frac{x+\alpha}{2}\right)\right]$.
What is $r$ equal to?
questions.solution:
Given that, $\int \frac{\mathrm{dx}}{\mathrm{a} \cos \mathrm{x}+\mathrm{b} \sin \mathrm{x}}=\frac{1}{\mathrm{r}} \ln \left[\tan \left(\frac{\mathrm{x}+\alpha}{2}\right)\right]$
Let $\mathrm{a}=\mathrm{r} \sin \alpha, \mathrm{b}=\mathrm{r} \cos \alpha\begin{aligned}
& \int \frac{d x}{r \sin \alpha \cos x+r \cos \alpha \sin x}=\frac{1}{r} \int \frac{1}{\sin (x+\alpha)} \\
& =\frac{1}{r} \int \operatorname{cosec}(x+\alpha) d x=\frac{1}{r} \ln \left[\tan \left(\frac{x+\alpha}{2}\right)\right]
\end{aligned}\begin{aligned}
& a=r \sin \alpha \Rightarrow a^2=r^2 \sin ^2 \alpha ...(i)\\
& b=r \cos \alpha \Rightarrow b^2=r^2 \cos ^2 \alpha...(ii)
\end{aligned}$
Adding (i) and (ii), we get
$\Rightarrow \quad \begin{aligned}
\mathrm{r}^2 & =\mathrm{a}^2+\mathrm{b}^2 \\
\Rightarrow \quad \mathrm{r} & =\sqrt{\mathrm{a}^2+\mathrm{b}^2} .
\end{aligned}$

questions.q:
What is $\int \frac{d x}{\sqrt{x^2+a^2}}$ equal to?
where $c$ is the constant of integration.
questions.solution:
$\begin{aligned} & \int \frac{d x}{\sqrt{x^2+a^2}} \\ & \text {Let } x=a \tan u \\ & \quad d x=a \sec ^2 u d u \\ & =\int \frac{a \sec ^2 u d u}{\sqrt{a^2 \tan ^2 u+a^2}} \\ & =a \int \frac{\sec ^2 u d u}{\sqrt{a^2\left(1+\tan ^2 u\right)}} \Rightarrow \frac{a}{a} \int \frac{\sec ^2 u d u}{\sec u}\end{aligned}\begin{aligned} & =\int \frac{\sec ^2 u d u}{\sec u}=\int \sec u d u \\ & =\ln [\tan (u)+\sec (u)]+c \quad\left[\because \int \sec x d x=\tan x\right]\end{aligned}\begin{aligned}
& =\ln \left[\frac{x}{\sqrt{a^2}}+\sqrt{1+\frac{x^2}{a^2}}\right]+c \\
& =\ln \left[\frac{x}{a}+\frac{\sqrt{a^2+x^2}}{a}\right]+c \\
& =\ln \left[\frac{x+\sqrt{x^2+a^2}}{a}\right]+c
\end{aligned}\therefore \quad$ Option (A) is correct.

questions.q:
Given that $\lim _{x \rightarrow \infty}\left(\frac{2+x^2}{1+x}-A x-B\right)=3$.
What is the value of A?
questions.solution:
$\begin{aligned}
& \lim _{\mathrm{x} \rightarrow \infty}\left(\frac{2+\mathrm{x}^2}{1+\mathrm{x}}-\mathrm{Ax}-\mathrm{B}\right)=3 \\
\Rightarrow & \lim _{\mathrm{x} \rightarrow \infty}\left(\frac{2+\mathrm{x}^2-\mathrm{Ax}-\mathrm{B}-\mathrm{Ax}^2-\mathrm{Bx}}{1+\mathrm{x}}\right)=3 \\
\Rightarrow & \lim _{\mathrm{x} \rightarrow \infty}\left[\frac{(1-\mathrm{A}) \mathrm{x}^2-(\mathrm{A}+\mathrm{B}) \mathrm{x}+2-\mathrm{B}}{1+\mathrm{x}}\right]=3
\end{aligned}$
Applying L'Hospital rule,
$2 x(1-A)-(A+B)=3$
Comparing coefficients
$\begin{array}{ll} 
& 2(1-A)=0 \\
\therefore \quad & A=1 \text { and } \\
& -(A+B)=3 \\
\therefore \quad & B=-3-1=-4 \\
& A+B=-3 \\
& A=1 . B=-4
\end{array}$

questions.q: If $E(\theta)=\left[\begin{array}{cc}\cos \theta & \sin \theta \\ -\sin \theta & \cos \theta\end{array}\right]$, then $E(\alpha) E(\beta)$ is equal to
questions.solution:
$\begin{aligned} & E(\theta)=\left[\begin{array}{cc}\cos \theta & \sin \theta \\ -\sin \theta & \cos \theta\end{array}\right] \\ & \text {Now } E(\alpha)=\left[\begin{array}{cc}\cos \alpha & \sin \alpha \\ -\sin \alpha & \cos \alpha\end{array}\right]\end{aligned}\begin{aligned}
& \text { and } E(\beta)=\left[\begin{array}{cc}
\cos \beta & \sin \beta \\
-\sin \beta & \cos \beta
\end{array}\right] \\
& \text { Now } E(\alpha) E(\beta)=\left[\begin{array}{cc}
\cos \alpha & \sin \alpha \\
-\sin \alpha & \cos \alpha
\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{cc}
\cos \beta & \sin \beta \\
-\sin \beta & \cos \beta
\end{array}\right] \\
& =\left[\begin{array}{cc}
\cos \alpha \cdot \cos \beta & \cos \alpha \sin \beta \\
-\sin \alpha \sin \beta & +\sin \alpha \cos \beta \\
-\sin \alpha \cos \beta & -\sin \alpha \sin \beta \\
-\cos \alpha \sin \beta & +\cos \alpha \cos \beta
\end{array}\right] \\
& =\left[\begin{array}{cc}
\cos (\alpha+\beta) & \sin (\alpha+\beta) \\
-\sin (\alpha+\beta) & \cos (\alpha+\beta)
\end{array}\right] \\
& =E(\alpha+\beta)
\end{aligned}\therefore \quad$ Option (C) is correct.

questions.q:
Consider the following in respect of two non-singular matrices $A$ and $B$ of same order:
1. $\operatorname{det}(A+B)=\operatorname{det} A+\operatorname{det} B$
2. $\quad(A+B)^{-1}=A^{-1}+B^{-1}$
Which of the above is/are correct?
questions.solution:
Non-singular matrix is a matrix whose determinate Value is non-zero.
Let $A=\left[\begin{array}{ll}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{array}\right]$ and $B=\left[\begin{array}{ll}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{array}\right]$
Here, $A$ and $B$ are non-singular matrix 
Now from Statement 1:
$\begin{aligned}
& A+B=\left[\begin{array}{ll}
1 & 1 \\
1 & 2
\end{array}\right]+\left[\begin{array}{ll}
2 & 1 \\
1 & 2
\end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{ll}
3 & 2 \\
2 & 4
\end{array}\right] \\
& \operatorname{det}(A+B)=12-4=8 \\
& \text { Now det }(A)=\left|\begin{array}{ll}
1 & 1 \\
1 & 2
\end{array}\right|=1 \\
& \text { and } \operatorname{det}(B)=\left|\begin{array}{ll}
2 & 1 \\
1 & 2
\end{array}\right|=3
\end{aligned}$
Now, $\operatorname{det}(A+B)=4 \neq \operatorname{det}(A+B)\therefore \quad$ Statement 1 is wrong.
Now from Statement 2:
$\begin{aligned}
& (A+B)^{-1}=\frac{1}{|A+B|} \operatorname{adj}(A+B) \\
& =\frac{1}{8}\left[\begin{array}{cc}
4 & -2 \\
-2 & 3
\end{array}\right] \\
& \text { and } \mathrm{A}^{-1}=\frac{1}{|\mathrm{~A}|} \operatorname{adj}(\mathrm{A})=\frac{1}{1}\left[\begin{array}{cc}
2 & -1 \\
-1 & 1
\end{array}\right] \\
& \text { and } B^{-1}=\frac{1}{|B|} \operatorname{adj}(B)=\frac{1}{3}\left[\begin{array}{cc}
2 & -1 \\
-1 & 2
\end{array}\right] \\
& \text { Now, } A^{-1}+B^{-1}=\left[\begin{array}{cc}
2 & -1 \\
-1 & 1
\end{array}\right]+\left[\begin{array}{cc}
\frac{2}{3} & \frac{-1}{3} \\
\frac{-1}{3} & \frac{2}{3}
\end{array}\right]
\end{aligned}=\left[\begin{array}{cc}
\frac{8}{3} & \frac{-4}{3} \\
\frac{-4}{3} & \frac{5}{3}
\end{array}\right] \neq(A+B)^{-1}\therefore \quad$ Statement 2 is wrong
$\therefore \quad$ Option (D) is correct.

& 3 p+q=5 ...(i)\\
& -4 p-q=2 ...(ii)\\
& 3 r+s=-2 ...(iii)\\
& -4 r-s=1...(iv)
\end{aligned}$
From equations (i) and (ii), we get
$\begin{array}{ll} 
& -p=7 \\
\therefore \quad & p=-7 \\
\Rightarrow \quad q=5-3(-7) \\

From equations (iii) and (iv),
$-r=-1\begin{aligned}
& \therefore \quad \mathrm{r}=1 \\
& \Rightarrow \quad \mathrm{~s}=-2-3=-5 \\
& \therefore \quad \mathrm{~s}=-5
\end{aligned}$
Hence, $A=\left[\begin{array}{ll}\mathrm{p} & \mathrm{q} \\ \mathrm{r} & \mathrm{s}\end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{cc}-7 & 26 \\ 1 & -5\end{array}$\right]\therefore \quad$ Option (A) is correct.

$\begin{aligned}
& =360-\left[4!\times \frac{3!}{2!}\right] \\
& =360-[24 \times 3] \\
& =360-72=288
\end{aligned}\therefore \quad$ Option (C) is correct.

only statement 2 is correct.

questions.q: If $2 p+3 q=18$ and $4 p^2+4 p q-3 q^2-36=0$, then what is $(2 p+q)$ equal to?

Putting the value of $q$ in $2 p+3 q=18\begin{aligned}
& 2 p+3 \times 4=18 \\
& 2 p=18-12 \\

& (2 p+q)=2 \times 3+4=10

$8+2=\frac{-b}{a} \Rightarrow \frac{b}{a}=-10$

$(-9) \times(-1)=\frac{c}{a} \Rightarrow \frac{c}{a}=9$
Putting value in original equation
$\begin{aligned}
& x^2+\frac{b}{a} x+\frac{c}{a}=0 \\
& x^2-10 x+9=0
\end{aligned}$

questions.q: What is the sum of the series $0.5+0.55+0.555+\ldots$ to $n$ terms?
questions.solution:
Given 0.5 + 0.55 + 0.555 + ..... to n
= 5 [0.1 + 0.11 + 0.111 + ..... to n terms]
$\begin{aligned}
& =\frac{5}{9}[0.9+0.99+0.999+\ldots . . \text { to } \mathrm{n} \text { terms }] \\
& =\frac{5}{9}\left[\frac{9}{10}+\frac{99}{100}+\frac{999}{1000}+\ldots . \text { to } \mathrm{n} \text { terms }\right]
\end{aligned}\begin{aligned} & =\frac{5}{9}\left(\left(1-\frac{1}{10}\right)+\left(1-\frac{1}{10^2}\right)+\left(1-\frac{1}{10^3}\right)+\ldots \cdot .\right. \\ & \left.\left(1-\frac{1}{10^{\mathrm{n}}}\right)\right] \\ & \quad=\frac{5}{9}\left[\mathrm{n}-\left(\frac{1}{10}+\frac{1}{10^2}+\ldots \cdot \frac{1}{10^{\mathrm{n}}}\right)\right]\end{aligned}=\frac{5}{9}\left[\mathrm{n}-\frac{1}{10} \frac{\left\{1-\left(\frac{1}{10}\right)^{\mathrm{n}}\right\}}{\left(1-\frac{1}{10}\right)}\right]=\frac{5}{9}\left[\mathrm{n}-\frac{1}{9}\left(1-\frac{1}{10^{\mathrm{n}}}\right)\right]$

questions.q: If $\log _{10} 2, \log _{10}\left(2^x-1\right)$ and $\log _{10}\left(2^x+3\right)$ are three consecutive terms of an A.P, then the value of $x$ is
questions.solution:
$\log _{10} 2, \log _{10}\left(2^{\mathrm{x}}-1\right)$ and $\log _{10}\left(2^{\mathrm{x}}+3\right)$ are in A.P. Hence, common difference will be same.
$\begin{aligned} \therefore & \log _{10}\left(2^{\mathrm{x}}-1\right)-\log _{10} 2=\log \left(2^{\mathrm{x}}+3\right)-\log _{10}\left(2^{\mathrm{x}}-1\right) \\ \therefore & \log _{10}\left(\frac{2^{\mathrm{x}}-1}{2}\right)=\log _{10}\left(\frac{2^{\mathrm{x}}+3}{2^{\mathrm{x}}-1}\right) \\ \Rightarrow & \frac{2^{\mathrm{x}}-1}{2}=\frac{2^x+3}{2^{\mathrm{x}}-1} \\ & \left(2^{\mathrm{x}}-1\right)^2=2\left(2^{\mathrm{x}}+3\right) \\ & 2^{2 \mathrm{x}}-2^{\mathrm{x}+1}+1=2^{\mathrm{x}+1}+6\end{aligned}2^{2 x}-2^{x+2}=5$
Let $2^x=y$, then
$\begin{aligned}
& y^2-4 y-5=0 \\
& y^2-5 y+y-5=0 \\
& y(y-5)+1(y-5)=0 \\
& y=-1, y=5
\end{aligned}$
Therefore, $2^{\mathrm{x}}=5x=\log _2 5$

Let $\alpha$ be the root of the equation $25 \cos ^2 \theta+5 \cos \theta-12=0$, 
where $\frac{\pi}{2} \lt \alpha \lt \pi$.
What is $\tan \alpha$ equal to?
questions.solution:
Here $\alpha$ is the root of equation
$25 \cos ^2 \theta+5 \cos \theta-12=0\begin{array}{ll}\Rightarrow \quad 25 \cos ^2 \alpha+5 \cos \alpha-12=0 \\ \Rightarrow \quad 25 \cos ^2 \alpha+20 \cos \alpha-15 \cos \alpha-12=0 \\ \Rightarrow \quad 5 \cos \alpha(5 \cos \alpha+4)-3(5 \cos \alpha+4)=0 \\ & (5 \cos \alpha-3)(5 \cos \alpha+4)=0 \\ & \cos \alpha=\frac{3}{5} \text { or } \cos \alpha=\frac{-4}{5}\end{array}$
Here, $\frac{\pi}{2} \lt \alpha \lt \pi\cos \alpha=\frac{-4}{5}$
( $\because$ In $2^{\text {nd }}$ quadrant, $\cos \alpha$ value is negative)
Now, $\sin \alpha=\sqrt{1-\cos ^2 \alpha}=\sqrt{1-\frac{16}{25}}\begin{aligned}
& \therefore \quad \sin \alpha=\frac{3}{5} \\
& \therefore \quad \tan \alpha=\frac{\sin \alpha}{\cos \alpha}=\frac{3}{5} \times \frac{-5}{4}=\frac{-3}{4}
\end{aligned}\therefore \quad$ Option (A) is correct.

questions.q: What is $\frac{\cos \theta}{1-\tan \theta}+\frac{\sin \theta}{1-\cot \theta}$ equal to?
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & \frac{\cos \theta}{1-\tan \theta}+\frac{\sin \theta}{1-\cot \theta} \\ & =\frac{\cos \theta}{1-\frac{\sin \theta}{\cos \theta}}+\frac{\sin \theta}{1-\frac{\cos \theta}{\sin \theta}} \\ & =\frac{\cos ^2 \theta}{\cos \theta-\sin \theta}+\frac{\sin ^2 \theta}{\sin \theta-\cos \theta}\end{aligned}\begin{aligned} & =\frac{\cos ^2 \theta}{\cos \theta-\sin \theta}-\frac{\sin ^2 \theta}{\cos \theta-\sin \theta} \\ & =\frac{\cos ^2 \theta-\sin ^2 \theta}{\cos \theta-\sin \theta}=\frac{(\cos \theta-\sin \theta)(\cos \theta+\sin \theta)}{\cos \theta-\sin \theta}\end{aligned}\therefore \quad$ Option (B) is correct.

questions.q:
If $\vec{a}+\vec{b}+\vec{c}=\overrightarrow{0}$, then which of the following is/are correct?
1. $\vec{a}, \vec{b}, \vec{c}$ are coplanar.
2. $\vec{a} \times \vec{b}=\vec{b} \times \vec{c}=\vec{c} \times \vec{a}$
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.solution:
According to statements (1) and (2),
when $\vec{a}+\vec{b}+\vec{c}=\overrightarrow{0}$, then both statements are correct.
If $\vec{a} \times \vec{b}=\vec{b} \times \vec{c}=\vec{c} \times \vec{a}=0$, then $\vec{a}, \vec{b}$ and $\vec{c}$ are collinear.
Therefore, option (C) is correct.
